samples.text:
The two pie charts shows which languages children in a city school district were speaking at home in 2005 and in 2025.

In 2005, most of children spoke only English at home, it was 78%. Spanish was 9%, and Polish and Mandarin were both 3%. Arabic was only 2% and other languages was 5%. So in that year only a small number of children spoke a different language in their home.

In 2025, English only was still the biggest group but it decreased to 61%. All other languages increased. Spanish went up to 12% and it was still the second. Polish grew to 7% and Arabic to 6%, so Arabic become three times bigger than 2005. Mandarin also increased a little to 5%, and other languages went up to 9%.

Overall, the English only speakers was the majority in both years, but the percentage of children who speak another language at home increased. This means the school district was more mixed in 2025 than in 2005.
samples.why: Relevant figures reported accurately · overview present at the end but somewhat general · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary with repetition · several article, agreement and tense errors which do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The pie charts illustrate the main languages spoken at home by children in a city school district in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, children who spoke only English at home made up the majority in both years, although their share fell considerably. Meanwhile, the proportions speaking every other language rose, making the district more linguistically diverse.

In 2005, more than three-quarters of children (78%) spoke only English at home. Spanish was the most common of the other languages, at 9%, followed by Polish and Mandarin, each at 3%, and Arabic at just 2%. Other languages together accounted for 5%.

By 2025, the percentage of English-only speakers had dropped to 61%. Spanish remained the second largest group, increasing to 12%. The most rapid growth, however, was seen in Arabic, which tripled from 2% to 6%, and Polish, which more than doubled to 7%. Mandarin rose more modestly to 5%, while the proportion speaking other languages increased to 9%. As a result, almost two in five children spoke a language other than only English at home by the end of the period.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main trend · key changes highlighted with accurate figures and derived comparisons · logical progression · range of cohesive devices · good vocabulary with one slightly awkward phrase.

samples.text:
The charts compare the languages that children in a city school district spoke at home in 2005 and 2025.

Although English-only households remained in the majority throughout, their share contracted markedly over the two decades, while every other language group expanded, pointing to a considerably more multilingual school population by 2025.

In 2005, English was the sole home language for 78% of children. Spanish was by far the most widely spoken alternative, at 9%, whereas Polish and Mandarin were each spoken by just 3% of pupils and Arabic by only 2%. Other languages accounted for the remaining 5%.

Twenty years later, the English-only group had fallen by 17 percentage points to 61%, meaning that the proportion of children speaking another language at home had risen from 22% to 39%. Spanish remained the leading minority language, edging up to 12%. The fastest growth, though, was in Arabic, which tripled to 6%, and Polish, which more than doubled to 7%, overtaking Mandarin in the process. Mandarin itself grew to 5%, and the combined share of other languages almost doubled, reaching 9%.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected · clear overview · accurate figures with purposeful derived comparisons (17 points, 22% to 39%) · smooth cohesion · precise vocabulary · wide range of accurate, complex structures.
